title: Free-body diagrams
examples: When should I draw a free-body diagram?
How do I show the direction of the forces?
Is the resultant force always drawn on the object?

explain.say: Today we are learning about free-body diagrams. These diagrams help us see all the forces acting on something. We will learn how to draw these forces correctly.
First, we must isolate the object we are studying. Imagine cutting the object away from everything else. This makes it easier to see only its forces.
Next, we draw the object as a simple dot or a box. We then draw arrows starting from this dot. Each arrow represents a single force acting on it.
The direction of the arrow is very important. For example, gravity always pulls straight down. Tension always pulls along the rope.
Finally, we find the resultant force. This is the single force that combines all the individual forces. We use vector addition to find this single net force.

faq.q: Do I have to draw the object itself in the diagram?
faq.a: No, you usually draw the object as a single point or a dot. This keeps the diagram simple and focuses only on the forces.
asks: Can I use a dot instead of a box?

faq.q: If two forces pull in opposite directions, how do I find the resultant?
faq.a: You subtract the smaller force from the larger force. The resultant force will point in the direction of the stronger force.
asks: Opposite forces, what do I do?
How do I calculate the net force between two opposing pulls?

faq.q: What does the length of the arrow represent?
faq.a: The length of the arrow must be proportional to the size of the force. A longer arrow means a bigger force.
asks: Does the arrow length mean anything?
How strong is the force shown by the arrow?

faq.q: When should I use a free-body diagram?
faq.a: You should use one anytime you need to analyze the forces acting on an object to find its acceleration. It is a planning tool for physics problems.
asks: Do I always need this diagram for dynamics problems?

faq.q: Is the resultant force always drawn pointing in the direction of motion?
faq.a: Not always. The resultant force points in the direction of the net acceleration. If the object is not accelerating, the resultant force is zero.
asks: Does the net force show where it goes?
If the object is still, what is the resultant force?

facts: A free-body diagram shows all forces acting on a single object.
Forces are represented by arrows, and the arrow's length shows the magnitude.
The resultant force is the vector sum of all individual forces.
If the resultant force is zero, the object is moving at a constant velocity.

quiz.say: A box is pulled horizontally by a force of ten newtons and is simultaneously pulled vertically by gravity, which is nine point eight newtons. What is the resultant force?
quiz.why: Since the horizontal pull is larger than the vertical pull, the resultant force will point in the direction of the larger force.

wrong.1: This is tempting because you added all the numbers together, but you must treat the directions separately.
wrong.2: This is wrong because the object is clearly being pulled in two different directions, so the net force is not zero.
wrong.3: This is wrong because it ignores the effect of gravity pulling the box downwards.

quiz.say: When drawing a free-body diagram for a book resting on a table, what two forces must you show?
quiz.show: Forces on a book on a table

options.show: Gravity down and Normal force up
options.say: Gravity down and Normal force up

quiz.why: Gravity pulls the book down, and the table pushes it up with a force called the normal force. These two forces balance each other.

wrong.0: Friction only acts when there is sliding or trying to slide, which is not happening when it rests.
wrong.1: This is too general; you must use the specific physics terms like 'Normal force' and 'Gravity'.
wrong.3: Tension is a pulling force usually associated with ropes or strings, which are not present here.

quiz.say: If you are analyzing a tug-of-war rope, and the forces pulling left and right are equal in magnitude, what is the resultant force?
quiz.why: When two forces are equal and opposite, they cancel each other out, meaning the resultant force is zero.

wrong.0: This is wrong because it ignores the equal and opposite force pulling to the right.
wrong.1: This is wrong because the forces are acting along a single straight line, not at an angle.
wrong.3: This is wrong because the forces are cancelling each other out, not adding up.
